items.title: [Bug]: /v1/unload_lora_adapter never removes the adapter from the engine
items.body:
### Your current environment

vLLM main (0.27.2rc0 at c0adee9231), Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B, `--enable-lora --max-loras 2 --max-cpu-loras 3`, `VLLM_ALLOW_RUNTIME_LORA_UPDATING=1`.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`POST /v1/unload_lora_adapter` only forgets the name on the frontend. It never tells the engine, so the adapter stays in the worker's GPU slot / CPU cache until LRU eviction gets to it.

`OpenAIServingModels.unload_lora_adapter` just does:

```python
del self.lora_requests[lora_name]
logger.info("Removed LoRA adapter: name '%s'", lora_name)
```

Nothing under `vllm/entrypoints/` calls `remove_lora`, even though `AsyncLLM.remove_lora` exists and the offline `LLM` API uses it. The Rust frontend's unload does call it, so the two frontends also disagree.

Repro:

1. Load `alice`, `bob`, `carol` via `/v1/load_lora_adapter`.
2. Unload `bob`. Returns `Success`, gone from `/v1/models`.
3. Worker still has `bob` on GPU (seen via `list_loras()` or the loaded-adapter metrics from #54830). It only goes away when a later load evicts it.

Why it matters: a GPU slot stays burned on something nobody can request, and unload + reload under the same name gets a fresh `lora_int_id`, so the worker caches both copies.

Expected: unload calls `engine_client.remove_lora(lora_int_id)` before dropping the registry entry. If keeping the weights cached is intentional, the endpoint should say so and the Rust frontend should match.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: KV offloading impossible for GLM-5.3 (DSA indexer): tail_cache block_size=4 fails the hash-alignment assertion, --mamba-cache-mode align does not reach it
items.body:
### Summary

KV offloading (`OffloadingConnector`, and by extension LMCache) cannot be enabled for
GLM-5.3-Flash because one of its KV-cache groups — the sparse-MLA indexer's **`tail_cache`** —
has `block_size=4` and cannot be aligned to the prefix-hash granularity. The assertion in
`offloading/config.py:55` rejects the whole configuration, and `--mamba-cache-mode align` does
not help because it does not reach this group.

The error message points the operator at `--enable-prefix-caching`, which is a dead end: prefix
caching is on by default and enabling it explicitly changes nothing.

### Reproduction

1× MI350X (gfx950), ROCm 7.2.3, vLLM `glm-release`, GLM-5.3-Flash (MXFP4), TP1,
`--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`, `--max-num-batched-tokens 32768`,
`--kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"OffloadingConnector","kv_role":"kv_both",
"kv_connector_extra_config":{"spec_name":"CPUOffloadingSpec","cpu_bytes_to_use":214748364800}}'`

```
AssertionError: tokens_per_block=4 not divisible by tokens_per_hash=8704.
  Hybrid models (e.g. Mamba+Attention) need --enable-prefix-caching to align block sizes.
```

Instrumenting `build_offloading_config` to print every group:

```
[GROUPS] tokens_per_hash=8704
[GROUPS]   UniformTypeKVCacheSpecs block_size=8704 -> tokens_per_block=8704  layers=24  first=...layers.3.self_attn.indexer.k_cache
[GROUPS]   UniformTypeKVCacheSpecs block_size=4    -> tokens_per_block=4     layers=12  first=...layers.3.self_attn.indexer.tail_cache
[GROUPS]   MambaSpec               block_size=8704 -> tokens_per_block=8704  layers=12  first=...layers.0.self_attn
[GROUPS]   MambaSpec               block_size=8704 -> tokens_per_block=8704  layers=11  first=...layers.1.self_attn
[GROUPS]   MambaSpec               block_size=8704 -> tokens_per_block=8704  layers=11  first=...layers.2.self_attn
```

Every group aligns to 8704 except `indexer.tail_cache`.

### Why `--mamba-cache-mode align` does not fix it

It does exactly what it promises, verified by instrumenting
`Platform._align_hybrid_block_size`:

```
[ALIGN] called. mamba_cache_mode='align' block_size=8704 mamba_block_size=16
[ALIGN] set: mamba_block_size=8704
```

`mamba_block_size` goes 16 → 8704 and the MambaSpec groups follow. But `tail_cache` is not a
Mamba group — it is a small per-sequence ring buffer holding recent raw K+gate to seed the
indexer's boundary pool (see the comment in `models/glm5next/nvidia/attention.py`: *"prefill
(seeds the boundary pool) and decode (per-step stash); read by the decode kernel to compress the
boundary pool"*). Nothing in the alignment path touches it, and semantically it has no
per-token block size to align.

With and without `--mamba-cache-mode align`, KV pool, timings and prefix-hit counts are
byte-identical (10,360,556 tokens; 2.25 s / 2.26 s / 0.75 s on a repeated 38k prompt), so the
flag is a no-op for this model apart from the mamba block size itself.

### Why this matters

Prefix caching on the GPU works well here — measured with a unique needle mid-context, hits read
from `vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total` (the API does not report `cached_tokens`):

| context | prefix hits from run 2 | share | needle |
|---|---|---|---|
| 60 000 | 147 968 → 513 536 | | 5/5 verbatim |
| 200 000 | 156 672 | 78 % | 5/5 verbatim |
| 600 000 | 478 720 | 80 % | 5/5 verbatim |

But it is bounded by GPU memory. The capacity argument for offloading is strong on this box:

| tier | capacity | 1M-token contexts |
|---|---|---|
| GPU (8 × 11.2M tokens) | 89.8M | 87 |
| host RAM (2 055 GB free) | 282M | 272 |
| disk (1.4 TB free) | 192M | 185 |

and a miss at 1M context costs **95.0 s** of prefill (measured, TP1) versus roughly 0.3 s to move
6.92 GB back over PCIe. That is the difference offloading would buy on long-context workloads.

### Suggested directions

1. **Let groups whose block size is smaller than `tokens_per_hash` opt out of offloading**
   rather than failing the whole configuration — but only if such a group can be *recomputed*
   rather than restored. For `tail_cache` that needs a maintainer's judgement: if the tail is not
   restored alongside the offloaded KV, the indexer's boundary pool is seeded from stale state
   and attention is silently wrong. **A blanket skip would trade a startup error for silent
   corruption, which is why I did not patch around it locally.**
2. **Fix the error message.** "need --enable-prefix-caching to align block sizes" sends the
   operator down a dead end when prefix caching is already enabled — which is the default. It
   would help to name the offending group and its layers.
3. If `tail_cache` genuinely cannot participate, it would be worth stating in the docs that
   KV offloading (and LMCache) is unavailable for DSA-indexer models, so operators do not spend
   time on it.

Happy to test a patch on this hardware — the setup above reproduces in one start.

items.title: [Bug]: qwen3_coder / qwen3_xml parser silently ignores tool_choice "required" and named function on /v1/chat/completions (0.28.0)
items.body:
### Summary

With `--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder` (or `qwen3_xml`, which maps to the same class), `tool_choice: "required"` and a named function `tool_choice` are not enforced on `/v1/chat/completions`. The request succeeds and the model behaves as if `tool_choice` were `"auto"`. Adding `"strict": true` to the tool does not change this.

This looks like the same root cause reported for gemma4 in #50477, poolside_v1 in #49712 and step3p5 in #51804, so it is not model specific. Filing separately because Qwen3 parsers are not mentioned in those threads.

### Environment

- vLLM 0.28.0 (PyPI wheel), torch 2.13.0+cu132, transformers 5.16.1, flashinfer-python 0.6.16.post3, xgrammar 0.2.3
- Python 3.12.14, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (sm_120), driver 580.105.08, single GPU
- Model: Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B (bf16), architecture Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration
- Flags: `--reasoning-parser qwen3 --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder --language-model-only --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --max-model-len 262144`
- `VLLM_ENFORCE_STRICT_TOOL_CALLING` left at default (True)
- Same behavior with the `vllm/vllm-openai:qwen38` Docker image

### Repro

Tools used in all requests:

```json
"tools": [
  {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "get_weather", "description": "Get current weather for a city",
    "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["city"]}}},
  {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "get_time", "description": "Get current local time for a city",
    "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["city"]}}}
]
```

All requests use `temperature: 0` and `chat_template_kwargs: {"enable_thinking": false}`. Results are the same with thinking enabled.

1. `tool_choice: "required"`, user message `Hi there!`

```json
{"finish_reason": "tool_calls", "message": {"content": "Hello! How can I help you today?", "tool_calls": null}}
```

No tool call was made, but `finish_reason` says `tool_calls`.

2. Same request with `"strict": true` on the tool and `max_tokens: 6`

```json
{"finish_reason": "length", "content": "Hello! How can I help", "tool_calls": null, "token_ids": [9419, 0, 2500, 628, 353, 1438]}
```

The very first generated token is prose, so no grammar was active.

3. Named function `tool_choice: {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "get_time"}}`, user message `What is the weather in Paris?`

```json
{"finish_reason": "stop", "message": {"content": "", "tool_calls": [{"function": {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": "{\"city\": \"Paris\"}"}}]}}
```

A different function than the one requested was called, and `finish_reason` is `stop`.

4. `tool_choice: "auto"` works as expected (single and parallel calls, streaming included). `response_format: {"type": "json_schema", ...}` also works, so structured output itself is functional on this setup.

The same three cases give the same results on `/v1/responses`.

### Expected

`required` should produce at least one tool call, a named function should produce a call to that function, or the server should return an error. A 200 with `finish_reason: "tool_calls"` and `tool_calls: null` is the worst of the options because clients treat it as a successful tool turn.

### Where the grammar gets lost (0.28.0)

Edited after more digging. An earlier version of this section said `adjust_request` is not called on the chat completions path. That was wrong: `vllm/renderers/online_renderer.py` does call `parser(...).adjust_request(request)` whenever `tool_choice != "none"` or a reasoning parser is configured. The grammar is lost inside the parser, not before it.

What I verified:

- The grammar itself is fine. `get_model_structural_tag(model="qwen_3_coder", tools=..., tool_choice="required", reasoning=False)` returns a `tags_with_separator` structural tag with `at_least_one: true`; for a named function it returns a single `tag`. If I put that exact structural tag into the request as `structured_outputs: {"structural_tag": ...}` together with `tools` and `tool_choice: "required"`, the server enforces it: the model emits `<tool_call>` XML, the parser extracts `get_weather({"city": "New York"})` and `finish_reason` is `tool_calls`. So the engine and xgrammar side works end to end.

- The parser used on the request path never attaches that grammar. `ParserManager.get_parser(tool_parser_name="qwen3_coder", reasoning_parser_name="qwen3", ...)` returns `Qwen3Parser`, whose `tool_parser_cls` is the generated `Qwen3ParserToolAdapter`. Running that parser's `adjust_request` offline on a `ChatCompletionRequest` with `tool_choice="required"` or a named function leaves `request.structured_outputs` as `None`, so `to_sampling_params()` produces no structured output constraint.

- Two things make that happen. `Qwen3ParserToolAdapter` has `structural_tag_model = None` and `supports_required_and_named = True` (class attributes checked at runtime), so `AbstractParser._apply_structural_tag` returns early. The `structural_tag_model = "qwen_3_coder"` and `supports_required_and_named = False` that are declared on `Qwen3EngineToolParser` (the class registered under the `qwen3_coder` and `qwen3_xml` names) are not on the adapter class that the request path instantiates. And `ParserEngineToolAdapter.adjust_request` (`vllm/parser/engine/adapters.py`) only forwards to `ParserEngine.adjust_request`, which sets `request.skip_special_tokens = False` and returns; it does not call `ToolParser.adjust_request`, so the JSON schema fallback for required/named (`get_json_schema_from_tools`) never runs either. Net effect: no grammar of either kind is attached for required or named tool_choice.

- Setting `structural_tag_model` and `supports_required_and_named` on `Qwen3ParserToolAdapter` alone does not fix it (tested offline, `structured_outputs` stays `None`), so the missing piece is in the parser engine's `adjust_request` path rather than just the class attributes.

Given that the explicit `structured_outputs.structural_tag` request works today, the fix looks like making the engine-based parser path build and attach the same structural tag that `get_model_structural_tag` already produces for `required` and named tool_choice.

Happy to test a patch. The three requests above are enough to reproduce, and the explicit structural tag request above is a working reference for the expected behavior.

items.title: [Bug][XPU] inductor-compiled decode pieces x speculative decode livelock both GPUs at >=32k ctx (graph capture alone clean; native stacks included)
items.body:
## Summary

With torch inductor compilation active for decode (`FULL_DECODE_ONLY` piecewise path) **combined with speculative decoding (MTP)**, both TP workers livelock permanently-ish at >=32k context: both GPUs show Compute Engines 100% + Copy Engines 100% (local spin, ~80 GB/s HBM, PCIe ~33 MB/s), host ranks park at the next device sync, and the engine stops serving. Whole-step XPU graph capture with eager kernels (`TORCH_COMPILE_DISABLE=1`) is fully clean through the same battery — the defect is the inductor-compiled region x spec decode, not XPU graph capture itself.

## Environment

- vLLM 0.21.1.dev0+gad7125a43 (XPU build) + vllm-xpu-kernels 0.1.8.3.dev0+g3cab97a
- torch 2.11.0+xpu, oneAPI 2025.3.2 / oneCCL 2021.15, NEO 37833, kernel 6.17.0-1010-intel
- 2x Intel Arc Pro B70 (BMG G31), TP=2
- Model: Qwen3.8-27B fp8 (GDN hybrid attention + MTP), `--kv-cache-dtype turboquant_4bit_nc`, `--block-size 512`, `--compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mode":"FULL_DECODE_ONLY"}'`, `--speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}'` (k=4 also reproduces the livelock but has a separate corruption bug, see #54785)

## Reproduction

Boot with the above flags; the compile+capture+spec posture is the wedging one (in our tree a fail-safe gate disables it; we use `VLLM_XPU_ALLOW_UNSAFE_SPEC_TP_GRAPH=1` to restore it for diagnosis). Then send **6 concurrent requests each with ~65k-token prompts and DIFFERENT prefixes** (cold prefills — prefix-cache-warm requests and single streams do not trigger it reliably). Within the first decode chunks both workers wedge: ttft climbs to ~200s, both GPUs spin.

## Discriminator matrix (each row a dedicated boot, same 65k battery)

| configuration | verdict |
|---|---|
| compile + capture + spec | WEDGE at 1st 65k chunk |
| + GDN ops split out of capture | wedges (already split by default) |
| + `moe_ops::moe_forward_full_fp8_block` split | wedges |
| + ALL custom ops split (`custom_esimd_kernels_vllm::*`, `_xpu_C::fp8_gemm*`) | wedges — every custom kernel exonerated |
| compile, no capture | WEDGE at chunk ~563 (slow onset) |
| **capture, NO compile (`TORCH_COMPILE_DISABLE=1`)** | **fully clean** (6/6 + 3/3 @65k + 10/10 canonical) |
| fully eager | clean |

Capture accelerates onset ~500x; it is an accelerator, not a necessary ingredient.

## Native stacks at the live wedge (gdb attached mid-stall)

Both TP workers' main threads parked **identically**:

```
#11 torch::jit::invokeOperatorFromPython(...)
#10 c10::Dispatcher::callBoxed(...)
#8  gdn_attention(...)                          [vllm_xpu_kernels/_xpu_C.abi3.so]
#7  gdn::chunk_gated_delta_rule_impl_xe2(...)   [vllm_xpu_kernels/libgdn_attn_kernels_xe_2.so]
#6  sycl::_V1::detail::queue_impl::wait(...)    [libsycl.so.8]
#2  v2::ur_queue_immediate_in_order_t::queueFinish()  [libur_adapter_level_zero_v2.so.0]
#1  ?? ()                                       [libze_intel_gpu.so.1]
#0  ?? ()                                       [libc]
```

The host is blocked in the **eager** GDN kernel's `q.wait()` on an **in-order** Level-Zero queue — i.e. work enqueued ahead of it on the same stream never retires while the device spins. Since the GDN kernel (and every other custom kernel) is exonerated by the split arms and capture-no-compile is clean, the never-retiring work is the inductor-compiled decode region sharing that stream. oneCCL is also exonerated (76,414/76,414 perfect eager all_reduce begin/end pairing per rank at a wedge; version-independent across 2021.15/2021.17.2).

## Workaround

`TORCH_COMPILE_DISABLE=1` with XPU graph capture left enabled: whole-step capture with eager kernels is clean through the full 65k battery and ~79% faster than fully-eager. We ship that as a fail-safe gate for spec+TP>1 in our image.

## Related

- #54785 — separate k=4 corruption under capture (compile-independent)
- oneCCL #212/#215 — our chase originally looked like their IPC-handle/allreduce hangs; cross-posted there as a triage datapoint (our case was NOT oneCCL)

items.title: [Bug][XPU] XPU graph capture + MTP num_speculative_tokens=4 produce non-deterministic, wrong logits at temperature=0 (k<=3 clean, eager clean, bs>=2 eager fallback clean, compile-independent)
items.body:
## Environment

- vLLM 0.21.1.dev0+gad7125a43 (XPU build) + vllm-xpu-kernels 0.1.8.3.dev0+g3cab97a
- torch 2.11.0+xpu, triton-xpu 3.7.0, oneAPI 2025.3.2 / oneCCL 2021.15
- 2x Intel Arc Pro B70 (Battlemage BMG G31, 8086:e223), NEO 37833, kernel 6.17.0-1010-intel
- Model: Qwen3.8-27B fp8 (GDN hybrid attention + MTP drafter heads), TP=2, `--kv-cache-dtype turboquant_4bit_nc`, `--block-size 512`, `--compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mode":"FULL_DECODE_ONLY"}'`, default XPU capture sizes (<=128), `--speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":4}'`

## Minimal repro (3 curls after one boot)

Boot the server (flags above), then send the SAME request 8x at temperature 0:

```bash
for i in $(seq 1 8); do
  curl -s http://localhost:8000/v1/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"model":"MODEL","prompt":"The capital of France is","max_tokens":6,"temperature":0,"logprobs":5}' \
    | python3 -c 'import sys,json; ch=json.load(sys.stdin)["choices"][0];
       top=sorted(((float(v),k) for k,v in (ch["logprobs"]["top_logprobs"][0] or {}).items()), reverse=True)[:2];
       print(repr(ch["text"]), ["%s:%.3f"%(k,v) for v,k in top])'
done
```

With k=4: outputs cycle between 2-3 variants (distinct >= 2); the top-1 logprob for the same position swings up to ~1.5 nats (-0.099 / -0.294 / -1.598 observed) and the top token itself can flip (' Paris' -> 'The'). After ~40 requests on the same boot, outputs degenerate (' France France France...').

Restart the SAME server with `num_speculative_tokens` = 3 (or 1, or 2): distinct = 1, top-1 logprob -0.451 bit-stable, all runs. That contrast is the whole bug report.

## What we established (each point from a dedicated boot/arm)

1. **The boundary is exactly k=4.** k=1/2/3 + graphs: distinct=1, top-1 -0.451 bit-stable, identical to the compile-no-capture reference (-0.453). k=4: corrupt. Not a gradient — a cliff.
2. **Capture is necessary.** `VLLM_XPU_ENABLE_XPU_GRAPH=0` + k=4 = deterministic (that is our reference number).
3. **Batch-size fallback is clean.** 2 concurrent requests on a capture-sizes-[1,2,4,8] boot (rows exceed the list -> eager fallback) both return the reference continuation. Corruption lives in the captured bs=1 pieces.
4. **Padding is NOT the trigger.** k=1 bs=3 (6 rows -> padded 8-piece) and k=2 bs=1 (3 rows -> padded 4-piece) are clean. The boundary tracks the draft-token count, not padded shape.
5. **Byte-reproducible.** Same responses in the same order across boots, across two image generations, and across capture lists [1..128] vs [1,2,4,8] — a deterministic function of request ordinal. The scheduler alternates among 2-3 execution paths and at least one computes wrong logits.
6. **temperature=0 IS honored**: a high-margin 40-token prompt returns 6/6 identical text even on a corrupt boot — the logits differ prompt-sensitively; this is not a sampler fault.
7. **Not a recent regression**: reproduces byte-for-byte on builds dating back ~4 image generations (>= v24-era, vLLM 0.21.1.dev line). Earlier "bare prompts are stable" observations were small-sample artifacts of the per-request-ordinal path cycling (a same-path run of 4 is unremarkable).
8. **Captured collectives are not required**: we do NOT run `VLLM_XPU_ALLOW_COMM_IN_GRAPH` (that mode returns deterministic garbage outright and is disabled); the corruption occurs with the default comm-outside-graph placement.
9. **Capture-level and COMPILE-INDEPENDENT (2026-09-01 discriminator)**: with `TORCH_COMPILE_DISABLE=1` and whole-step XPU graph capture still on (dynamo/inductor never engage — pure eager kernels inside the captured step), k=4 STILL corrupts: distinct=3 across 8 identical requests, top-1 logprob drifting (-1.668 / -0.187 / -0.050 at the same position), no wedge through the full 65k battery. k<=3 under the identical posture is bit-stable == eager reference. This rules the inductor-compiled pieces OUT of this bug (in contrast to the separate 65k livelock we chased on the same stack, which WAS convicted to inductor x spec) and pins the defect to the capture/replay of multi-draft-position spec state.
10. **Deployed mitigation**: we clamp `num_speculative_tokens` 4 -> 3 with a boot warning whenever any graph capture is active and a speculative config is present (escape hatch env for repro: `VLLM_XPU_ALLOW_K4_CAPTURE=1`). k=3 retains most of the MTP speedup at bs=1 for us.

## Suspect area

Multi-draft-position spec machinery under graph capture/replay (capture-level, not inductor — see datapoint 9) — the same machinery as the GDN spec-kernel ragged-batch OOB we previously found and fixed locally (wheel rebuild): GDN speculative state buffers and/or the verify mask for 4 draft positions, as replayed inside FULL_DECODE_ONLY pieces. k<=3 clean / k=4 corrupt / bs>=2-eager clean / padding-refuted together point at state that is sized or advanced per draft position and not correctly reset or re-bound between piece replays.

## Impact

Any XPU user running MTP k=4 with graphs (the shipped default combination for our config) gets silently wrong greedy outputs. Throughput/stability testing does not catch it — every historical arm of ours measured wedges and token rates only, and all of those k=4 arms almost certainly served corrupt text.

## Related

- #26963 (speculative decoding support on XPU — tracking issue)

items.title: [RFC] Bounded, restart-safe capacity management for the filesystem KV offload tier
[RFC]: GDS kv offloading
items.body:
## Motivation

vLLM KV cache offloading persists KV cache blocks from device (GPU, TPU, etc) to slower storage (CPU memory, NVMe, object stores) and loads them back on demand. We intend to add GDS (GPUDirect Storage) as a primary tier alongside CPU offloading. 

A large part of this work involves the refactoring of the existing cpu offloading.  Specifically, the `OffloadingWorker` interface passes logical device block IDs to workers, which then internally resolve them to device pointers. This duplicates tensor layout logic in every worker implementation. As part of our GDS implementation, we refactor the worker interface so that device pointer resolution happens once (at the `OffloadingConnectorWorker` boundary) and workers receive pre-resolved device pointers.

To further facilitate code reuse, we also introduce `FSOffloadingWorker`, an abstract base for file-based device offloading, so that different filesystem backends (GDS/cuFile, POSIX, NIXL, etc.) can be added without duplicating logic.

## Goals:

- GDS supports both read and write
- GDS supports canonical and TP agnostic
- GDS supports cross layout. Traditional per-layer contiguous layout might require a bounce buffer.
- Maximize code reuse between cpu offloading and gds offloading

## High level design

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        Scheduler Process                             │
│  **Shown for completeness, we do not change this process.**             │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │           OffloadingConnectorScheduler                         │  │
│  │                                                               │  │
│  │  • Decides which blocks to offload/load                       │  │
│  │  • Constructs DeviceLoadStoreSpec (block_ids, group_sizes, ...)  │  │
│  │  • Calls manager.prepare_store()                              │  │
│  │        → OffloadingLoadStoreSpec (polymorphic)                 │  │
│  │          resolved to CPULoadStoreSpec or FSLoadStoreSpec       │  │
│  │  • Packs into TransferJob(src_spec, dst_spec)                 │  │
│  │                                                               │  │
│  └───────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                              │                                       │
│                              │ TransferJobs serialized into           │
│                              │ OffloadingConnectorMetadata            │
└──────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────┘
                               │
                               │  IPC (scheduler → worker process)
                               ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         Worker Process (Device)                       │
│                                                                      │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │           OffloadingConnectorWorker                             │  │
│  │                                                                │  │
│  │  • Receives TransferJobs containing DeviceLoadStoreSpec           │  │
│  │  • Holds CanonicalKVCaches (device tensor references)          │  │
│  │  • Maps: DeviceLoadStoreSpec → DevicePointers                 │  │
│  │  • Calls worker.submit_store(job_id, device_ptrs, dst_spec)    │  │
│  │  • Calls worker.submit_load(job_id, src_spec, device_ptrs)     │  │
│  │  • Polls worker.get_finished() for completion                  │  │
│  │                                                                │  │
│  └─────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                │                                      │
│                                │ submit_store / submit_load           │
│                                ▼                                      │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │                    OffloadingWorker (ABC)                       │  │
│  │                                                                │  │
│  │  submit_store(job_id, device_ptrs: DevicePointers,             │  │
│  │               dst_spec: OffloadingLoadStoreSpec) -> bool       │  │
│  │  submit_load(job_id, src_spec: OffloadingLoadStoreSpec,        │  │
│  │              device_ptrs: DevicePointers) -> bool              │  │
│  │  get_finished() -> list[TransferResult]                        │  │
│  │  wait(job_ids: set[int]) -> None                               │  │
│  │  shutdown() -> None                                            │  │
│  │                                                                │  │
│  ├────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┤  │
│  │                        │                                       │  │
│  │  CPUOffloadingWorker   │   FSOffloadingWorker (ABC)            │  │
│  │                        │       │                               │  │
│  │  • Device ↔ CPU DMA    │       ├── GDSOffloadingWorker         │  │
│  │                        │       │   (cuFileWrite/Read)          │  │
│  │                        │       ├── PosixOffloadingWorker       │  │
│  │                        │       │   (pread/pwrite, future)      │  │
│  │                        │       └── NIXLOffloadingWorker         │  │
│  │                        │           (NIXL, future)              │  │
│  │                        │                                       │  │
│  └────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Worker Class Hierarchy

```
OffloadingWorker (ABC)
│
├── CPUOffloadingWorker
│   • Device ↔ CPU pinned memory DMA
│   • Receives: DevicePointers + CPULoadStoreSpec
│   • Resolves CPU block_ids → CPU tensor pointers internally
│   • Executes: swap_blocks_batch on device stream
│
└── FSOffloadingWorker (ABC)
    • Device ↔ filesystem (common orchestration)
    • Receives: DevicePointers + FSLoadStoreSpec (keys)
    • Groups pointers per key, resolves keys → file paths via FileMapper
    • Manages thread pool, completion tracking, file handle lifecycle
    • Delegates actual I/O to subclass abstract methods
    │
    ├── GDSOffloadingWorker
    │   • cuFileWrite / cuFileRead (device-direct DMA to NVMe)
    │   • Registers device buffers with cuFileBufRegister at init
    │   • No CPU bounce buffer — true zero-copy
    │
    ├── PosixOffloadingWorker (future)
    │   • pread / pwrite with CPU bounce buffer
    │   • Works on any POSIX filesystem
    │
    ├── NIXLOffloadingWorker (future)
    │   • NIXL FILE→VRAM transfers
    │
    └── CUDAFileOffloadingWorker (future)
        • cuFile async API (stream-ordered)
```

## Component Interactions (Store Path)

```
 OffloadingConnectorScheduler          OffloadingConnectorWorker
 ─────────────────────────────         ─────────────────────────────
 1. Selects blocks to offload
 2. device_spec = DeviceLoadStoreSpec(
        block_ids=[0,1,2],
        group_sizes=[3],
        block_indices=[0])
 3. dst_spec = manager.prepare_store()
        → OffloadingLoadStoreSpec (polymorphic)
          e.g. CPULoadStoreSpec(block_ids=[5,6,7])
          or   FSLoadStoreSpec(keys=[key0, key1, key2])
 4. Packs TransferJob
                    ──── IPC ────►     5. Receives TransferJob
                                       6. device_ptrs = resolve_device_pointers(
                                              device_spec, self.kv_caches)
                                       7. worker.submit_store(
                                              job_id, device_ptrs, dst_spec)
                                                    │
                                                    ▼
                                       CPUOffloadingWorker:
                                         • src = device_ptrs.ptrs (device addrs)
                                         • dst = resolve CPU block_ids
                                               → CPU tensor pointers
                                         • swap_blocks_batch(src, dst, sizes)

                                       ── OR ──

                                       GDSOffloadingWorker (via FSOffloadingWorker):
                                         • Groups device_ptrs per key
                                         • For each key:
                                           path = file_mapper.get_file_name(key)
                                           cuFileWrite(dev_ptr, size, file_offset)
```

## Component Interactions (Load Path)

```
 OffloadingConnectorScheduler          OffloadingConnectorWorker
 ─────────────────────────────         ─────────────────────────────
 1. Identifies blocks to load
 2. device_spec = DeviceLoadStoreSpec(
        block_ids=[10,11,12],
        group_sizes=[3],
        block_indices=[0])
 3. src_spec = manager.prepare_load()
        → OffloadingLoadStoreSpec (polymorphic)
          e.g. CPULoadStoreSpec(block_ids=[5,6,7])
          or   FSLoadStoreSpec(keys=[...])
 4. Packs TransferJob
                    ──── IPC ────►     5. Receives TransferJob
                                       6. device_ptrs = resolve_device_pointers(
                                              device_spec, self.kv_caches)
                                       7. worker.submit_load(
                                              job_id, src_spec, device_ptrs)
                                                    │
                                                    ▼
                                       CPUOffloadingWorker:
                                         • src = resolve CPU block_ids
                                         • dst = device_ptrs.ptrs (device addrs)
                                         • swap_blocks_batch(src, dst, sizes)

                                       ── OR ──

                                       GDSOffloadingWorker (via FSOffloadingWorker):
                                         • Groups device_ptrs per key
                                         • For each key:
                                           path = file_mapper.get_file_name(key)
                                           cuFileRead(path → dev_ptr, size, offset)
```

## FSOffloadingWorker Internal Design

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  FSOffloadingWorker (ABC)                                         │
│                                                                  │
│  Owned state:                                                    │
│  • file_mapper: FileMapper          (key → path resolution)      │
│  • block_size_factor: int           (device blocks per file)     │
│  • thread_pool: ThreadPoolExecutor  (async I/O submission)       │
│  • transfers: dict[job_id, _Transfer]  (in-flight tracking)      │
│                                                                  │
│  submit_store(job_id, device_ptrs, dst_spec):                       │
│    1. Groups device_ptrs into per-key chunks                        │
│       (using group_block_counts + group_data_ref_counts)         │
│    2. For each key in dst_spec.keys:                             │
│       • Builds ops: list[(dev_ptr, size, file_offset)]           │
│       • Submits to thread pool: self.write_block(path, ops)      │
│    3. Records futures in _Transfer for completion tracking       │
│                                                                  │
│  submit_load(job_id, src_spec, device_ptrs):                        │
│    (mirror of submit_store)                                      │
│                                                                  │
│  get_finished() / wait() / shutdown():                           │
│    (common future-based completion tracking)                     │
│                                                                  │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Abstract methods (subclass implements):                    │  │
│  │                                                            │  │
│  │  write_block(path, ops: list[(dev_ptr, size, offset)])     │  │
│  │  read_block(path, ops: list[(dev_ptr, size, offset)])      │  │
│  │  init_backend(kv_caches)  ← optional setup (buf register) │  │
│  │  shutdown_backend()       ← optional cleanup               │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         │                              │
         ▼                              ▼
┌──────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────┐
│  GDSOffloadingWorker │    │  PosixOffloadingWorker   │
│                      │    │  (future)                │
│  init_backend:       │    │                          │
│    cuFileDriverOpen  │    │  write_block:            │
│    cuFileBufRegister │    │    os.pwrite(fd, buf,    │
│                      │    │      offset)             │
│  write_block:        │    │    (with CPU bounce buf) │
│    fd = open_for_gds │    │                          │
│    h = HandleRegister│    │  read_block:             │
│    cuFileWrite(...)  │    │    os.pread(fd, size,    │
│    HandleDeregister  │    │      offset)             │
│    os.close(fd)      │    │    cudaMemcpy → GPU      │
│                      │    │                          │
│  read_block:         │    └──────────────────────────┘
│    fd = open_for_gds │
│    h = HandleRegister│
│    cuFileRead(...)   │
│    HandleDeregister  │
│    os.close(fd)      │
│                      │
└──────────────────────┘
```


## TP agnostic related changes

To enable larger IO when reading or writting TP agnostic data, we propose writing TP agnostic data in the following order: layer, head, chunk. This is a change from the way TP agnostic data is writen today, which is: block, head, layer.

## Access mode

Introduce access mode offloading connector parameter which can be read, write, or readwrite (which is the default). This facilitates multi-connector setup using multi-tier and gds, where the multi tier writes to the file system and the gds connector reads.  We suggest enabling access mode for the multi-tier fs secondary connector and gds.

## Key Design Decisions

1. **Changes are resticted to the worker** - we avoid making changes in
   the scheduler or to the multi-tier logic. An exception can be made for
   introducing a write_only mode to the multi-tier secondary storage.

2. **`DeviceLoadStoreSpec` stays at the scheduler level** — the scheduler thinks
   in block IDs. Resolution to device pointers happens once at the
   `OffloadingConnectorWorker` boundary via `resolve_device_pointers()`.

3. **Code reuse** - a prime goal of this work is to avoid code duplication
   between the cpu offloading and gds offloading

4. **`FSOffloadingWorker` as ABC** — common file-based offloading logic
   (key→path mapping, per-key pointer grouping, thread pool, completion
   tracking) lives in the base class. Subclasses implement only
   `write_block`/`read_block`.

---

### Proposed Change.

two weeks

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@Etelis @orozery @dannyharnik @maheshrbapatu


### Any Other Things.

This RFC intends to include the work described in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48504.

items.title: [Bug]: KDA/gated-delta-rule chunked-scan buffers are outside memory profiling — runtime OOM at large --max-num-batched-tokens
items.body:
### Summary

The chunked-scan buffers in the gated-delta-rule (KDA) path scale linearly with
`--max-num-batched-tokens`, are allocated transiently inside the forward pass, and are **not
covered by vLLM's startup memory profiling**. The KV cache is therefore sized as if that memory
were free, and above a certain chunk size the engine dies at runtime — mid-request, after having
served traffic.

### Observed

GLM-5.3-Flash (45 layers: 34 KDA linear-attention + 11 sparse MLA), 1× MI350X (gfx950),
ROCm 7.2.3, TP1, MXFP4 weights, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`, `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.93`.
16 concurrent requests of ~38k tokens each.

| `--max-num-batched-tokens` | successful | failed | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 192 … 65 536 | 16 / 16 | 0 | stable across 3 runs each |
| **81 920** | **5 / 16** | **11** | engine shut down |
| **131 072** | **4 / 16** | 12 | engine shut down |

```
(Worker) ERROR  File ".../flash_linear_attention/ops/chunk_delta_h.py", line 357,
                  in chunk_gated_delta_rule_fwd_h
(Worker) ERROR    v_new = torch.empty_like(u) if save_new_value else None
(Worker) ERROR  torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 1.25 GiB.
                  GPU 0 has a total capacity of 287.98 GiB of which 0 [bytes is free]
(APIServer) INFO [shutdown] EngineCore process manager: using 15.0s ROCm cleanup grace
                  after immediate request abort
```

Startup reported no problem — `GPU KV cache size: 6,940,947 tokens` at 81,920, and the memory
profiling line looked healthy.

### Mechanism

`chunk_gated_delta_rule_fwd_h` allocates two buffers proportional to the token count in the batch:

```python
B, T, Hg, K, V = *k.shape, u.shape[-1]
H  = u.shape[-2]
BT = chunk_size                      # FLA_CHUNK_SIZE = 64, hard-coded in ops/utils.py:31
...
N, NT = len(cu_seqlens) - 1, len(chunk_indices)
h     = k.new_empty(B, NT, H, V, K)          # NT = ceil(T / 64)  -> linear in T
v_new = torch.empty_like(u) if save_new_value else None   # linear in T
```

For this model (`linear_attn_config`: 64 heads, head_dim 128) at T = 81,920 with BT = 64:

```
NT     = 1280
h      = 1280 · 64 · 128 · 128 · 2 B  ≈ 2.5 GiB
v_new  = 81920 · 64 · 128 · 2 B       ≈ 1.25 GiB   <- the allocation that failed
```

That is ~3.75 GiB transient **per KDA layer invocation**, and there are 34 KDA layers per forward
pass. They are freed between layers, so the caching allocator mostly reuses the blocks — but the
peak is real, and it is not what the profiling run measured. Measured peaks from vLLM's own log,
same model, same everything but the chunk size:

```
chunk  8 192:  14.52 GiB peak activation   KV 9,578,037 tokens
chunk 65 536:  22.73 GiB peak activation   KV 7,512,186 tokens
```

The KV pool shrinks ~35 KV-tokens per extra chunk token, linearly, which is the profiler
*partially* accounting for this. But at 131,072 the loss jumps to ~60 KV-tokens per chunk token —
non-linear — and at 81,920 the runtime allocation no longer fits.

### Why it matters beyond this model

The failure mode is the bad one: **it does not fail at startup, it fails under load.** A
configuration passes a smoke test, serves requests, then the engine dies with requests in flight.
And it is silent in the metrics — `vllm bench serve` computes `Total input tokens` over
*successful* requests only, so throughput per second goes **up** as requests die. In my own sweep
81,920 initially looked like the fastest setting (+21 % over baseline) purely because 11 of 16
requests never completed.

Any model with gated-delta-rule / linear-attention layers goes through this path (GLM-5.x hybrid,
Qwen3-Next GDN, and others).

### Suggested directions

1. **Include the KDA path in the memory profiling run** at the configured
   `max_num_batched_tokens`, with a batch composition representative of chunked prefill
   (several sequences, not one), so the peak is measured rather than partly inferred.
2. **Or bound the buffers**: `FLA_CHUNK_SIZE` is a module-level constant
   (`third_party/flash_linear_attention/ops/utils.py:31`). Making it configurable would let
   operators trade chunk-scan parallelism for memory — `BT = 128` halves `h`. `BT` is already a
   free `tl.constexpr` in the kernels (the `64` in the block pointers is the head-dim blocking,
   not the time chunk), so this looks mechanically possible, though I have not yet measured
   whether 128 is correct and faster.
3. **Or refuse the configuration at startup** rather than at runtime, if the peak can be
   computed analytically from `max_num_batched_tokens`, the head count and `FLA_CHUNK_SIZE`.

Happy to test a patch on this hardware.

**Unrelated but adjacent, in case it helps someone sizing a config:** the ~11.7 GiB left unused by
`--gpu-memory-utilization 0.93` on a 288 GiB part is *not* free headroom — it is where these
transient allocations land. vLLM's own log suggests `--kv-cache-memory=<the full amount>` to
"fully utilize gpu memory"; taking that suggestion at a large chunk size is what removes the room
this path needs.

items.title: [RFC]: Custom all-reduce for XPU
items.body:
### Motivation.

On 2x Intel Arc Pro B70, TP=2 runs at **61.4% of a single card** (17.5 vs 28.5 tok/s, Qwen3.8-27B GPTQ INT4, eager, no spec decode). Communication volume is not the reason: decode moves 1.29 MB/token over a link measured at 28.6 GB/s, so roughly 45 µs of wire time against a 47 ms step.

The cost is per *invocation*, not per byte. Each collective issues 85 to 91 Level Zero API calls regardless of message size, and a 0-byte `barrier()` costs the same 88 calls and 41.9 µs as a 10 KiB all-reduce. 24 of those calls are `zeDeviceGetCommandQueueGroupProperties`, a static device property that is re-queried every time. Decode issues 129 collectives per token, so this is paid 129 times per token with nothing to amortise it against.

There is a second, independent cost. The collective is synchronous on the host: `dist.all_reduce` blocks the calling thread for its full duration (measured, issue time equals completion time), so in eager mode the host stalls for 129 x 17 to 56 µs per token.

<details>
<summary>Measurements</summary>

2x Intel Arc Pro B70, PCIe Gen5 x8 (28.65 GB/s H2D measured), 600.3 GB/s VRAM read. `vllm/vllm-openai-xpu:nightly-7c5dc571` (unpatched upstream, vLLM 0.28.1rc1.dev199, vllm-xpu-kernels 0.1.14.1), Qwen3.8-27B GPTQ INT4, `--enforce-eager --max-model-len 8192 --max-num-seqs 1`, 300 tokens x2.

**Level Zero calls per collective** (2 ranks, bf16, torch profiler):

| call | per collective | note |
|---|---|---|
| `zeDeviceGetCommandQueueGroupProperties` | 24.00 | invariant across 10 KiB / 100 KiB / 1 MiB and `barrier()` |
| `zeEventQueryStatus` | 24 to 33 | completion spin; 173 at 1 MiB |
| `zeMemGetAllocProperties` | 13.00 | invariant |
| others | ~28 | |
| **total** | **85 to 91** | a single matmul costs 8.96 |

**Host cost** (10 KiB all-reduce, 2 ranks):

| | latency | CPU |
|---|---|---|
| `dist.all_reduce` (oneCCL) | 56.0 µs | 98.2 µs |
| `barrier()` (0 bytes) | 41.9 µs | |

CPU exceeds latency for oneCCL because a spin thread burns a second core.

**End-to-end**, TP=2, `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.45`:

| | tok/s | vs TP=1 |
|---|---|---|
| TP=1 (util 0.90) | 28.48 | 100% |
| TP=2 oneCCL | 17.49 | 61.4% |

**Profile** (50 tokens, rank 0): `vllm::all_reduce` accounts for 2422 ms of a 9.10 s window over 6450 calls, which is 129 per token. Both ranks are symmetric within 2%, so this is not straggler skew. Device (`kernel`) time drops from 1780 to 1126 ms as expected for TP=2, while host `cpu_op` time rises from 7489 to 13327 ms.

</details>

### Proposed Change.

Add an opt-in XPU device communicator that bypasses oneCCL for `all_reduce`, following the shape of `custom_all_reduce.py` (CUDA, #2192) and `quick_all_reduce.py` (ROCm, #19744):

* Level Zero IPC gives each rank direct access to the peer's device buffer. dma-buf FDs are exchanged once at init over a UNIX socket (`SCM_RIGHTS`) and cached.
* Reduction is one-shot, as CUDA does for `world_size == 2`.
* The rank handshake happens **inside the kernel** via flags in IPC-shared device memory, so the host enqueues and returns (CUDA's `Signal` / `RankSignals`). Above 128 KiB the kernel's PCIe read (~12 GB/s) loses to the copy engine (~28 GB/s), so larger messages take a host-synchronised path instead.
* Single opt-in flag, **default off**. Degrades from device-sync to host-sync to oneCCL on any failure, with both ranks agreeing before switching.
* Scope: `all_reduce` only, `world_size == 2`, single node. Everything else goes to oneCCL.

Measured effect with the linked Draft PR: **17.5 to 28.5 tok/s (+62.9%)**, which puts TP=2 at parity with a single card. With MTP speculative decoding (built into Qwen3.5/3.8), **30.8 to 47.3 tok/s (+53.7%)**, which puts TP=2 5.5% ahead of a single card. Per-collective host cost drops from 56.0 to 6.8 µs.

### Would fixing oneCCL be better?

For the first half of the problem, yes. The 24 redundant property queries are an oneCCL/UR issue, and fixing them there would benefit every XPU user including ones not on this path. I would rather that happened. But it does not address the second half. `dist.all_reduce` blocking the host is why CUDA and ROCm both carry their own implementations, and making oneCCL cheaper does not remove it.

### Alternatives considered

* **Host shared-memory staging** instead of IPC: works and needs no C++ extension, but at 1 MiB it is indistinguishable from oneCCL (296.0 vs 294.8 µs), and it cannot move the handshake off the host. Dropped.
* **A wrapper around an existing library**, as `aiter_custom_all_reduce.py` does for AMD: I could not find such a library for XPU.

### Feedback Period.

No deadline on my side. The Draft PR is there to try; I will keep it rebased while this is open.

### CC List.

@mayuyuace @chaojun-zhang @jikunshang @xinyu-intel @YizhouZ

### Any Other Things.

A Draft PR with a working implementation is open at #54768 . It is 578 lines of Python excluding kernels, which is over the 500 LOC threshold in CONTRIBUTING, hence this RFC.

I am an external contributor with a pair of B70s as my only test hardware, so the scope above (all_reduce, world_size == 2, single node) reflects what I can verify rather than what the design could cover.

I found no prior or in-flight work on this in either repo. If I missed something, please point me at it.

## AI assistance


The investigation and the linked implementation were done with Claude Code (Opus 5 directing and measuring, Fable 5 implementing), with the human author choosing the problem and scope, rejecting conclusions the data did not support, and reviewing the result. The measurements above were produced and cross-checked in that loop; details are in the PR.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: ModelOpt NVFP4 checkpoint with an FP8-quantized PLE n-gram table fails to load (ngram_embedding.weight_scale)
items.body:
### Your current environment

vLLM `nightly-7c5dc571cbd1064ecc8a9b1045637ff647aa22cb` (2026-09-01, first build after #53896
merged) and the pre-merge branch build `vllm/vllm-openai:qwen38-flash-next` (2026-08-26).
2x NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (SM120, 96 GB), TP=2, CUDA 13.

### What happened

Loading `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` fails at 203 of 206 shards:

```
ValueError: There is no module or parameter named 'ngram_embedding.weight_scale' in
Qwen4ExpNGramEmbedding. The available parameters belonging to ngram_embedding
(PLEVocabParallelEmbedding) are: {'ngram_embedding.weight'}
```

### Why

The checkpoint is quantized with NVIDIA ModelOpt to NVFP4, and its `hf_quant_config.json`
lists `"*.ple.*"` in `ignore` — the PLE n-gram table is quantized *separately* to FP8. In the
weight map it appears as its own `model-plefp8-*.safetensors` shards with exactly one global
`ngram_embedding.weight_scale`, which is precisely the layout
`Qwen4ExpPLEFp8EmbeddingMethod` ("FP8 PLE embedding with one global checkpoint scale") is
written for.

That method is never selected, because `_get_ple_embedding_quant_method` in
`vllm/models/qwen4_exp/nvidia/ple_layer.py` gates on the *whole* checkpoint being FP8:

```python
if not isinstance(quant_config, Fp8Config):
    return None
```

Under a ModelOpt NVFP4 config the plain embedding path is built, no `weight_scale` parameter
is registered, and the loader raises. `Qwen4ExpPLEFp8EmbeddingMethod.create_weights` reads no
field of `quant_config`, so the gate is the only obstacle — selecting the method makes the
checkpoint load.

Everything else about the checkpoint works: the architecture is recognised, the ModelOpt
config is auto-detected (`Detected ModelOpt NVFP4 checkpoint (quant_algo=NVFP4)`) and the MoE
picks real NVFP4 kernels (`Using 'FLASHINFER_CUTLASS' NvFp4 MoE backend`).

### Why it matters

This mixed layout is what makes the model fit on two 96 GB cards: 125.9 GiB with the FP8 PLE
table, against 170-174 GiB for the NVFP4 requantizations that keep the PLE in bf16
(`primitive-ai/…`, `Inferact/…`) and 172.8 GiB for `Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8`. At
`--gpu-memory-utilization 0.93` two cards give a 177.8 GiB budget, so only the FP8-PLE variant
leaves room for a KV cache. `VLLM_PLE_CPU_OFFLOAD` needs ~95 GiB of host RAM for a bf16 table,
and the disk-backed variants (#54129, #54070) are not merged.

### Suggested fix

Let the selector accept a checkpoint whose PLE shards carry a global `weight_scale` even when
the top-level quantization is not `Fp8Config` — detected from the weight map, or gated behind
an explicit flag. Note that a bf16 PLE table can appear under the same ModelOpt config, so the
decision cannot be made from `quant_config` alone.

Happy to open a PR if the maintainers agree on how the detection should work.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Searched open and closed issues; the closest are #53908 (auxiliary-GPU PLE offload),
      #53960 (`VLLM_PLE_CPU_OFFLOAD` deadlock) and #54426 (fp8 KV on the QSA path), none of
      which cover this.

items.title: [Bug]: PLE short-conv batched prefill pads all requests to batch-max query length, causing transient activation OOM on mixed-length workloads(Qwen3.8-Flash-Next)
items.body:
### Your current environment

Summary

The PLE dilated short-conv batched prefill path for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next packs all prefill requests of a step into a dense tensor of shape `(num_prefills, max_prefill_query_len, hc_hidden_size)`, where `max_prefill_query_len` is the **batch-max** query length. Activation memory therefore scales with `num_prefills × batch_max_len`, independent of the actual number of tokens scheduled. On mixed-length production traffic this can inflate activation transiently by ~10x over the profiling estimate and crash the engine with CUDA OOM while the KV cache is only ~13% utilized.

## Environment

- vLLM: 0.1.dev20073+g8e685d198 (vllm/vllm-openai:qwen38-flash-next image)
- Model: Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 (local path), config: hidden_size=2560, hc_count=4 → hc_hidden_size=10240
- Hardware: 4× H200 140GB, tensor-parallel-size 4 + expert-parallel 4, MTP speculative decoding (num_speculative_tokens=5)
- Engine args: `--max-num-batched-tokens 32768 --max-num-seqs 32`, chunked prefill enabled (default)

## Crash

```
(Worker_TP1_EP1) torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 4.78 GiB.
GPU 1 has a total capacity of 139.80 GiB of which 3.91 GiB is free.
...
File ".../vllm/models/qwen3_8_flash_next/nvidia/ple_layer.py", line 842
    return torch._C._nn.silu(input)
```

Scheduler log of the crashing step:

```
num_scheduled_tokens = {...: 11, ...: 1352, ...: 4, ...: 10, a3b0...: 31344, ...: 4, ...: 8, ...: 9, ...: 10, ...: 15}
total_num_scheduled_tokens = 32767
num_computed_tokens = [51170, 47164, 86768, 56976, 23032, 41608, 96608, 147992, 39200]
SchedulerStats(num_running_reqs=10, num_waiting_reqs=1, kv_cache_usage=0.1319)
```

## Trigger

Mixed-length production traffic (multi-turn agents):

- A fresh 153,853-token prompt enters the waiting queue; the scheduler assigns it a 31,344-token chunk (budget 32,768).
- 7 other sessions are concurrently appending context (multi-turn continuations with high prefix-cache hit rate, ~84%); their prefill chunks are tiny (4–1,352 tokens).
- All 10 requests are packed into one step. `max_prefill_query_len = 31,344` → **every row** (including the 7 tiny ones) is padded to 31,344.
- Slot matrix: 8 × 31,344 × 10,240 × bf16 = **4.78 GiB per intermediate**; ~2–3 intermediates alive along the short-conv path (`packed_tokens` → `.transpose(1,2).contiguous()` → `history` cat → `conv1d` → `silu`) → ~12 GiB transient vs ~11.8 GiB free → OOM.

Why standard benches do not catch it: with equal-length prompts (32K×32, 100K×8, etc.) padding waste ≈ 0 and the activation peak matches the profiling run. Only mixed-length batches with a long chunk + several short chunks blow it up. Any multi-turn agentic workload with concurrent long-prompt arrivals reproduces this.

### 🐛 Describe the bug


## Root cause (source-level)

`vllm/models/qwen3_8_flash_next/nvidia/ple_layer.py`:

- Line ~791: `max_len = metadata.max_prefill_query_len` (batch max, CPU-computed to avoid device sync)
- Line ~802: `packed_tokens = x_p.new_zeros((num_prefills, max_len, hidden_size))` — dense row-per-request packing
- Line ~842: `conv_output = F.silu(conv_output).transpose(1, 2).contiguous()` — allocation site of the failing 4.78 GiB tensor

`hidden_size` here is `hc_hidden_size = config.hidden_size × config.hc_count = 2560 × 4 = 10,240`, and `key_proj`/`value_proj` are `ReplicatedLinear` — **not TP-sharded**, so every card allocates the full-width buffer. With TP4, each of the 4 ranks independently allocates the same 4.78 GiB.

Aggravating factors:

1. Padding ratio is unbounded: a single long chunk inflates the row width for all co-scheduled short chunks (in the crash step: 1,424 real tokens padded to 31,344 → ~22× per row).
2. `long_prefill_token_threshold` (scheduler) caps per-request chunk length and therefore bounds `max_len`, but it is off by default and its interaction with this packing is undocumented.
3. The profiling/warmup run at startup uses a single large equal batch, so the measured activation peak (≈4 GiB) is far below the mixed-batch worst case (≈12 GiB transient) and vLLM reserves the rest for KV pool accordingly.

## Comparison: KDA/GatedDeltaNet (GLM-5.3-Flash) does not have this problem

The GatedDeltaNet-based linear attention (e.g. `glm5next/nvidia/kda.py`, used by GLM-5.3-Flash) processes batched prefill via **varlen compact layout with `cu_seqlens`** (see kda.py ~line 594) — activation scales with the actual token count, no per-row padding. Its conv channels are also TP-sharded (64 heads × 128 dim / TP4 = 2,048 per rank). Under the same adversarial schedule the peak activation is ~0.3 GiB. GLM runs fine at gpu_memory_utilization=0.9 with high concurrency; Qwen3.8-Flash-Next OOMs at 0.85.

## Suggested fix

- Preferred: rework PLE short-conv batched prefill to a varlen/compact packing keyed by `cu_seqlens` (as done in the GatedDeltaNet path), eliminating the `(num_prefills, max_len, hidden)` dense buffer entirely.
- Interim: cap `max_prefill_query_len` inside the PLE metadata builder (equivalent to enforcing `long_prefill_token_threshold` per chunk), or document `--long-prefill-token-threshold` as required for this model and add a mixed-length activation-profiling mode at startup.

## Workaround we validated (analysis-level)

`--long-prefill-token-threshold 8192` + `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.82` bounds the worst-case slot matrix to ~8×8,192×10,240×2B×~2.5 ≈ 3 GiB, well within the post-0.82 free margin, at the cost of ~1.5–2× TTFT for cold prompts longer than 8K tokens.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: On ROCm, DCP and non-FP8 KV dtypes are unreachable, but the errors suggest fixes that don't exist there
items.body:
### Your current environment

8x AMD MI350X (gfx950), ROCm 7.2.3, vLLM with AITER. Model: GLM-5.3 (`glm_moe_dsa` → `deepseek_v32` → on ROCm the generic `deepseek_v2.GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM`), TP4, MXFP4 experts + FP8 attention, `fp8_e4m3` KV cache.

### Describe the bug

Two capabilities that would raise KV-cache capacity are reachable in the CLI but cannot work on ROCm, and the error messages point users toward a fix that does not exist on this platform.

**1. DCP: the error suggests switching backends, but no ROCm backend qualifies.**

`v1/worker/cp_utils.py:47`:

```
AssertionError: Decode Context Parallelism (DCP) requires attention implementations
to return the softmax LSE during decode, but ... does not.
Try a different backend by setting --attention-backend or disable DCP.
```

Counting `need_to_return_lse_for_decode` across all 22 files in `v1/attention/backends/mla/`:

| backend | LSE occurrences | ROCm/AITER/HIP mentions |
|---|---:|---:|
| `rocm_aiter_mla_sparse` | **0** | 53 |
| `rocm_aiter_mla` | **0** | 99 |
| `aiter_triton_mla` | **0** | 7 |
| `cutlass_mla` | 3 | 0 |
| `flashmla_sparse` | 3 | 0 |
| `flashattn_mla` | 2 | 0 |
| `flashinfer_mla_sparse` | 2 | 1 |
| `flashinfer_mla`, `flashmla`, `tokenspeed_mla` | 1 | 0 |

Every LSE-capable MLA backend is CUDA-only. And vLLM itself reports at startup:

```
Using ROCM_AITER_MLA_SPARSE backend out of potential backends: ['ROCM_AITER_MLA_SPARSE']
```

There is exactly one candidate on ROCm for this model, and it does not return LSE. So `--attention-backend` cannot resolve the assertion — the suggestion sends users looking for something that isn't there.

Before hitting this, there is a second, separate hurdle worth noting: the model requests `q_replicate=True` through `verify_and_update_config` (visible as `dcp_comm_backend=a2a` instead of the default `ag_rs`), and `mla_attention.py:1096` then raises `NotImplementedError: DCP query replication is not implemented for the aiter ...`. That one **is** avoidable with `VLLM_DCP_Q_REPLICATE=0`, per the comment in `deepseek_v2.py:1049` ("The env var predates the config field and still wins if set explicitly"). The LSE assertion is what remains.

**2. Non-FP8 KV cache dtypes fail with a generic message.**

`CacheDType` in `config/cache.py` lists 18 values. Three tried on this setup, all with the same result:

```
--kv-cache-dtype fp8_ds_mla           ValueError: No valid attention backend found for rocm with ...
--kv-cache-dtype int4_per_token_head  ValueError: No valid attention backend found for rocm with ...
--kv-cache-dtype turboquant_k8v4      ValueError: No valid attention backend found for rocm with ...
```

The message names neither which dtypes *are* supported on the platform nor that the limitation is platform-wide rather than model-specific.

### Suggestion

Not asking for the features themselves — this is about discoverability:

1. Make the DCP assertion platform-aware: when no LSE-capable backend exists for the current platform, say so instead of suggesting `--attention-backend`.
2. Have the KV-dtype validation list the dtypes the resolved backend actually accepts.

Both would have saved a couple of hours here, and the information is already available at the point where the errors are raised.

### Scope of what I verified

Verified: the counts above from the source tree, that `VLLM_DCP_Q_REPLICATE=0` clears the first hurdle, and that DCP=2 and DCP=4 both stop at the LSE assertion. Not verified: whether adding LSE to the ROCm backends is straightforward — I did not read the AITER kernels closely enough to judge that.

items.title: [RFC]: The dynamic-SD K decision is a batch-keyed array index — agreeing on its shape before more signals arrive
items.body:
### Motivation.

On current `main` (`504bb8b0c3`) the dynamic-SD K decision is one array index:

```python
# vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:1321-1324
if self.dynamic_sd_lookup is not None and len(num_scheduled_tokens) > 0:
    num_spec_tokens_to_schedule = self.dynamic_sd_lookup[
        len(num_scheduled_tokens)
    ]
```

The key is batch size, and that choice is fixed in four places, not one:

- `validate_and_normalize_dynamic_sd_schedule` unpacks entries as
  `(range_start, range_end, num_speculative_tokens)` (`dynamic/utils.py:37`)
- `build_dynamic_sd_schedule_lookup` returns `list[int]`, a dense
  `batch_size -> K` table (`dynamic/utils.py:77-81`)
- the scheduler indexes it by `len(num_scheduled_tokens)` (`sched/scheduler.py:1322`)
- since #50488, two capture-planning sites read the same dense table
  (`worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py:219`, `config/vllm.py:2067`)

The decision site is not short of information — `schedule()` has the request set
in hand, so per-request `num_computed_tokens`, acceptance history and queue
depth are all in scope. They are simply not read. Whatever a proposal wants K to
depend on, it currently has to widen that tuple everywhere, or bypass the
schedule entirely.

**Six different signals are being proposed for this one decision right now.**
Batch size is what ships. Beyond it:

| signal | where |
|---|---|
| context length | #48944 (mine), widening the tuple to `(bs, ctx) -> K` |
| token entropy | #54082, gating K between 0 and K at runtime |
| marginal gain | LibraSpec, [2608.08721](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08721) |
| expert activation cost | EcoSpec, [2607.12696](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12696) |
| step-wise efficiency (entropy-controlled length) | SparseSpec-L, [2607.27735](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27735) |
| learned verification payoff | Hybrid Verified Decoding, [2606.01019](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01019) |

Two of those papers converge on the same criterion. SparseSpec-L states it
directly: *"extending the speculation horizon can reduce rather than improve
speedup when the marginal acceptance probability falls below the relative
drafting cost."*

I am not asking for any of them to be adopted. I am asking whether the K
decision should keep being a batch-keyed array index, given that the next six
proposals all need it not to be.

### Evidence I can offer, with its limits.

I ran the (batch, ctx) case, so the numbers below are about that one signal.
Full provenance, including what I have withdrawn, is in a
[ledger](https://github.com/seongyun1104/depthchart/blob/931ff25/EVIDENCE_LEDGER.md);
the per-cell working is in a
[companion note](https://github.com/seongyun1104/depthchart/blob/931ff25/POLICY_INTERFACE.md).

**1. The win localises to a single cell.** Position-balanced 2 trials, cache
wiped per launch, cold-start burn, 3 warm-up discarded + 3 measured per cell,
c=256, per-arm stdev at most 1.72 %, Gemma-4-31B-it-QAT-FP8 with its assistant
drafter on one H100 NVL. A batch-only schedule `[[1,64,3],[65,128,1],[129,512,0]]`
against a (bs, ctx) schedule that differs from it in exactly one cell — at
bs ≥ 129 and ctx ≥ 769, K=3 instead of K=0:

| ctx | batch-only | (bs, ctx) | ratio |
|---:|---:|---:|:-:|
| 400 | 1875.6 | 1890.7 | 1.01× |
| 900 | 1453.5 | 1874.6 | 1.29× |
| 1900 | 1416.6 | 1848.2 | 1.30× |
| 4000 | 1232.8 | 1680.4 | 1.36× |

The ctx=400 tie is the design working: there both schedules select K=0. The
mechanism is narrow and worth stating plainly — **at high batch a batch-only
schedule has to turn speculation off, and context is what tells you when to turn
it back on.**

The distinct-K set is `{0, 1, 3}` for both schedules, so this costs no extra
CUDA graphs; graphs are keyed on K, and the K values are the same ones.

**2. A cost model over the same interface gets that cell wrong.** I also have a
producer that derives the schedule from a stated cost model rather than typing
it — `K* = argmax_K E_accept(K) / (F(ctx) + K·M(bs))`, the same marginal-utility
shape LibraSpec and SparseSpec-L arrive at. Run with the coefficients it ships,
sweeping only the acceptance prior across 0.35–0.75 (the campaign observed
44–47 % in the K=3 tier), it selects **K=0 at the high-batch tier at every
context**. It reproduces the batch-only schedule and would not have found the
cell worth 29–36 %.

That gap closes under recalibration — the per-context coefficient has to be
roughly an order of magnitude larger relative to the per-batch one — not under a
change of functional form. I am reporting it because it is the honest state of
that producer: a stated model, uncalibrated, currently disagreeing with my own
measurement.

**3. What I have not established.** One model pair, one hardware configuration,
one concurrency, four context points, one differing cell. I have not calibrated
the cost model on hardware. I have not attributed the DSD baseline tax to its
terms — the 2×2 design for that is written and unrun. And the sharpness of the K
optimum at low batch did not clear its own pre-registered bar (#48627, and see
the ledger); the result above is at c=256, which is a different regime.

### Proposed Change.

**None yet — this asks for a decision, not a design.** I have a stake here
(#48944 is the ctx-axis version) and I would rather the shape be agreed before
more signals arrive than argue for mine.

The question is where the K decision should live:

1. **Keep it batch-keyed** and let each new signal negotiate its own widening.
   Predictable, and the dense array stays trivially cheap. #50488 has just made
   this the assumption in two more places, so this is the status quo by default
   rather than by decision.
2. **Let the schedule declare its own key set**, so `(bs, ctx)` and any later
   key are the same kind of object to the consumers. This is what #48944 does
   for one extra key; generalising it is a small change to the validator, the
   lookup and the three read sites.
3. **Separate the decision from the schedule**, so that a table, a cost model,
   or a runtime controller are interchangeable producers of K. Two producers
   already exist behind one schedule in my branch, which is the minimum evidence
   for this being more than speculative generality — but two is also the
   minimum, and I would not argue for it on that basis alone.

What I think matters more than which option: **nothing in the engine currently
measures the quantity these policies need.** Acceptance is exported in aggregate,
but per-`(batch bucket, ctx bucket, K)` draft and verify latency, first-rejection
position, committed tokens per verification, and K-keyed graph hit/miss are not.
My cost model missed the cell above because its coefficients were guesses; there
is no way to stop them being guesses from inside vLLM today. If only one thing
comes out of this thread, that telemetry is the one I would pick, and it is
independent of which option above wins.

I have opened #54748 for the smallest piece of it, so this is not a request for
someone else to do the work: steps the schedule sends to K=0 build no
`SpecDecodingStats` at all, so a schedule that has correctly stopped speculating
under load is indistinguishable from speculative decoding not running. That PR
adds a step counter keyed on the selected K and is deliberately independent of
everything proposed here.

### Feedback Period.

No deadline. I will not open a PR against any of the three options without
agreement here first.

### Any Other Things.

Related: RFC #48627 (the ctx axis specifically, with its evidence section
corrected on 2026-09-01), PR #48944, #54082, #49986, #49548, #48494.

Prior art on the ctx dependence itself: MagicDec
([blog](https://infini-ai-lab.github.io/MagicDec-part1/), paper
[2408.11049](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.11049)) proposes choosing speculation
amount as a function of sequence length; TurboSpec/SmartSpec
([2406.14066](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.14066)) is the batch-adaptive
predecessor of the schedule API this RFC is about.
